title: Searchable symmetric encryption
description: SSE lets a server search encrypted documents for keywords without decrypting them: the client builds an encrypted index, the server matches trapdoors to index entries. Email and file hosts use it — search works, the server learns only the access pattern (which documents matched), not the content.
method: Build an encrypted inverted index client-side; upload; search via trapdoors; the server returns matching (encrypted) documents.
usage: Accept the access-pattern leakage consciously; pad or obfuscate queries for sensitive searches.

demo.code:
print('index: enc("urgent") -> [doc3, doc7] (server sees ciphertext)')
print('search "urgent": trapdoor -> server returns docs 3,7 (content hidden)')

title: Deterministic encryption for equality
description: Deterministic encryption (same plaintext -> same ciphertext) enables equality queries on encrypted columns: 'find all records with this encrypted SSN'. It leaks equality patterns, so it's for low-sensitivity equality matching with the tradeoff stated explicitly — CryptDB's onion layers work this way.
method: Encrypt deterministically (e.g., AES-SIV); the database indexes ciphertext; equality queries work; document the leakage.
usage: Use only where equality queries are required; state the leakage; prefer randomized encryption elsewhere.

demo.code:
print('enc(ssn) deterministic -> index lookup works')
print('leakage: equal SSNs visible as equal ciphertexts (documented)')

title: Metadata minimization
description: The best encrypted metadata is no metadata: minimization asks what tags are truly needed and deletes the rest. Every tag is a liability (even encrypted, it leaks existence and size); the minimization review regularly prunes tags nobody uses.
method: Inventory all metadata; justify each tag's existence; delete unjustified tags; review quarterly.
usage: Default to fewer tags; each new tag needs a written justification.

demo.code:
print('metadata inventory: 47 tags')
print('review: 12 unjustified -> DELETED; 35 kept with reasons')

title: Key management for metadata keys
description: Encrypted metadata multiplies keys: per-tag keys, per-role keys, rotation schedules. KMS-backed envelope encryption with automatic rotation keeps this manageable — data keys encrypted by master keys in the HSM, rotated on schedule, old versions retained for decryption.
method: Envelope encryption; HSM master keys; automatic rotation; retain old key versions for reading old data.
usage: Automate rotation; never lose old key versions while old data exists; audit key usage.

demo.code:
print('tag key v3 (current), v1-v2 retained for old tags')
print('rotation: automatic 90d; usage logged to KMS audit')

title: Traffic-analysis resistance
description: Even encrypted tags leak via traffic analysis: message sizes, timing, frequencies. Resistance means padding to uniform sizes, batching and mixing sends, and cover traffic — making the observable pattern reveal nothing. The metadata's metadata needs protection too.
method: Pad to fixed sizes; batch sends; add cover traffic; randomize timing within bounds.
usage: Apply where the adversary watches the network; measure the overhead honestly.

demo.code:
print('all messages padded to 4KB, sent in 5-min batches')
print('observer sees: uniform blobs on schedule (nothing else)')

title: Zero-knowledge tag proofs
description: Prove a tag satisfies a policy without revealing the tag: 'this document is releasable to role X' proved in zero knowledge. The verifier learns the authorization decision, not the classification details — need-to-know enforced cryptographically.
method: Commit to the tag; prove the policy predicate in ZK; the verifier checks the proof, learns only the decision.
usage: Use for cross-domain authorization where tag values are themselves sensitive.

demo.code:
print('prove: clearance(tag) >= required (ZK)')
print('verifier: AUTHORIZED (tag value unseen)')

title: Encrypted tagging for classification
description: Documents carry encrypted tags (classification level, project code) that only authorized classifiers can read or match. Routing and access decisions use the tags without exposing them to the infrastructure — the mailroom sorts sealed envelopes by their wax seals.
method: Encrypt tags with ABE or per-role keys; infrastructure matches ciphertext tags to routing rules; content stays sealed.
usage: Separate tag keys from content keys; rotate tag keys on role changes.

demo.code:
print('tag enc("top-secret") routable by mailroom (sees: project-X sealed)')
print('content key: separate, held by cleared analysts only')

title: Order-preserving encryption
description: OPE preserves order: enc(a) < enc(b) iff a < b, enabling range queries on encrypted data. It leaks order (inherently), so modern guidance prefers it only where range queries are essential and the leakage is modeled — again CryptDB's approach with explicit leakage analysis.
method: Encrypt with an order-preserving scheme; B-tree indexes work on ciphertext; analyze and document order leakage.
usage: Use only for required range queries; model the leakage; consider alternatives (ORAM, trusted hardware).

demo.code:
print('enc(25) < enc(40): range query [20,50] works on ciphertext')
print('leakage: order visible (accepted for this column, documented)')
